specPoints.text: know that esters contain the functional group
know that ethyl ethanoate is the ester produced when ethanol and ethanoic acid react in the presence of an acid catalyst
understand how to write the structural and displayed formulae of ethyl ethanoate
understand how to write the structural and displayed formulae of an ester, given the name or formula of the alcohol and carboxylic acid from which it is formed and vice versa
know that esters are volatile compounds with distinctive smells and are used as food flavourings and in perfumes

primer.text: From Reactions of Carboxylic Acids you already know the -COOH group giving salts with metals and carbonates. This note introduces a gentler partner: alcohols, which join the acid directly and build the sweet-smelling ester family used across kitchens and perfume counters.

lessons.title: Making esters from alcohols and acids
sourceHeadings: Diagram showing the formation of ethyl ethanoate
lessons.opening: Alcohols and carboxylic acids join hands in an esterification reaction, releasing water as they bond. The product carries the -COO- link and, for the two smallest partners, the sweet oily liquid called ethyl ethanoate. This lesson draws the functional group and the equation that balances both products.
keyPoints: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid react to make an ester in an esterification reaction.
Esters carry the functional group R-COO-R between two carbon chains.
Ethanoic acid with ethanol and a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst gives ethyl ethanoate.
The equation reads CH3COOH + C2H5OH giving CH3COOC2H5 + H2O.
A molecule of water is released as the two reactants join.

low.restatement: An alcohol plus a carboxylic acid makes an ester, with water also formed. Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyses the joining, and the smallest pairing gives ethyl ethanoate.
low.analogy: The reaction is two hands locking: the alcohol hand and the acid hand clasp, and a water molecule slips away like a dropped glove.
low.examPointer: State both products every time: the ester and the water.

medium.restatement: Esterification joins an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, with concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst, and releases one water molecule per bond formed. Ethanoic acid with ethanol yields CH3COOC2H5, the ester ethyl ethanoate of the two smallest partners.
medium.analogy: Picture the acid handing over one -OH and the alcohol one -H to build water, while their remaining skeletons clip together through the -COO- link.
medium.examPointer: Write the equation with both reactants and both products; omitting the water is the common mark-loser.

check.stem: Which two families of compound react to make an ester?

options.text: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Those are exactly the two reactants the esterification recipe calls for.
That pairing makes an alcohol by hydration, not an ester.
That pairing releases carbon dioxide and builds a salt, not an ester.
Substitution with halogens builds haloalkanes, a different family.

check.stem: What else is produced alongside the ester during esterification?

options.explanation: One -H and one -OH leave the reactants as a water molecule for every ester link made.
Hydrogen belongs to acid-metal reactions, not to esterification.
No carbonate is present, so no carbon dioxide can form.
The reaction is a joining that always pays for itself with water.

check.stem: Which catalyst is used when ethanol and ethanoic acid make ethyl ethanoate?

options.explanation: The strong acid catalyses the joining without being consumed.
Phosphoric acid catalyses ethene hydration, a different process.
Enzymes belong to fermentation, not to ester-making.

options.text: No catalyst is needed at all
options.explanation: Without the acid catalyst the reaction is impractically slow.

check.stem: Which arrangement marks a compound as an ester?

options.text: A -COO- link sitting between two carbon chains
options.explanation: The R-COO-R arrangement is the ester signature.
That is the carboxylic acid group, the reactant rather than the product.
A lone -OH marks an alcohol.
A C=C marks an alkene and plays no part in the ester group.

check.stem: Which ester is produced from ethanol and ethanoic acid?

options.explanation: The alcohol gives ethyl and the acid gives ethanoate, in that order.
Methyl would need methanol, one carbon shorter than ethanol.
Methanoate would need methanoic acid, one carbon shorter than ethanoic.
Propyl would need propanol, one carbon longer than ethanol.

lessons.title: Naming esters and their everyday uses
lessons.opening: Ester names read backwards from their making: the alcohol lends its -yl part first, the acid lends its -oate part second. The family smells sweet, evaporates readily and turns up in flavourings and perfumes. This lesson turns names into structures and back again.
keyPoints: The first part of an ester name comes from the alcohol and ends in yl.
The second part comes from the carboxylic acid and ends in oate.
Pentanol reacting with butanoic acid gives pentyl butanoate.
Esters are volatile liquids with distinctive, sweet smells.
Their uses include food flavourings and perfumes.

low.restatement: Ester names take yl from the alcohol and oate from the acid: pentanol plus butanoic acid gives pentyl butanoate. The liquids are volatile, sweet-smelling and used in flavourings and perfumes.
low.analogy: A name is a handover note: the alcohol signs first in yl, the acid countersigns in oate, and the flavour bottle shelves the result.
low.examPointer: When converting a name back, split it at yl and oate before drawing anything.

medium.restatement: The alcohol chain supplies the yl segment and the acid chain the oate segment, so pentanol with butanoic acid yields pentyl butanoate. Members are volatile liquids with strong sweet smells, which is why they serve as food flavourings and perfume ingredients.
medium.analogy: Volatility is the delivering power of the liquid: molecules leave the surface readily and ride the air to the nose, the whole trick behind a perfume.
medium.examPointer: Expect name-to-structure and structure-to-name in both directions; practise until the split at yl and oate is automatic.

check.stem: Which ester forms from methanol and ethanoic acid?

options.explanation: One-carbon alcohol gives methyl, two-carbon acid gives ethanoate.
Both halves are shifted: the reactants are reversed in size.
The acid half stays ethanoate because ethanoic acid supplies it.
That ester needs ethanol, one carbon longer than methanol.

check.stem: An ester is named propyl methanoate. Which two reactants made it?

options.explanation: Propyl points to a three-carbon alcohol and methanoate to the one-carbon acid.
That pair would be named methyl propanoate, the mirror mix-up.
Ethanol lends ethyl, not propyl.
The acid half would then read propanoate, not methanoate.

check.stem: Why are esters chosen for perfumes?

options.text: They are volatile with distinctive pleasant smells
options.explanation: Easy evaporation carries the scent, and the smells are exactly the sweet kind wanted.

options.text: They are the cheapest liquids available
options.explanation: Cost is not the stated reason; smell and volatility are.

options.text: They are completely unreactive on skin
options.explanation: Inertness is not the property being exploited in perfumery.
Solvent power over salts is irrelevant to perfume use.

check.stem: In the name butyl propanoate, what does the butyl part describe?

options.text: The four-carbon chain donated by the alcohol
options.explanation: The yl segment always reports the alcohol side of the ester.

options.text: The chain donated by the acid
options.explanation: The acid side is always reported in the oate segment.
Water takes no part in ester naming.
Catalysts never appear in the product name.

check.stem: Which statement about the volatility of esters is correct?

options.text: Their low boiling points let vapours reach the nose readily
options.explanation: Volatility means easy evaporation, which delivers the scent efficiently.

options.text: They never evaporate at room temperature
options.explanation: Volatility means precisely that they do evaporate readily.
Esters boil below water in many cases, which is why they smell at all.

options.text: Volatility makes them gases at room temperature
options.explanation: They are described as oily liquids that evaporate easily, not as gases.

glossary.definition: The reaction in which an alcohol and a carboxylic acid join to make an ester, releasing water.
A compound carrying the -COO- link between two carbon chains, usually sweet-smelling and oily.
The ester formed when ethanol and ethanoic acid react in the presence of an acid catalyst.
The -COO- bridge through which the two reactant chains are clipped together.
Turning to vapour easily at low temperature, which carries the smell to the nose quickly.
